title: Leave what makes you doubt
hookLine: leave what makes you doubt for what doesn't
tomorrow: what could you quit today that makes your faith better?

cards: The milk smells slightly off. Not sour, exactly. You stand at the open fridge and sniff it again, and a third time, and you still can't say.

Yesterday's question asked for one short line for every gray area. Al-Hasan ibn Ali says he memorized it from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Leave what makes you doubt for what doesn't make you doubt.

teach.b: Notice the shape of it. It doesn't ask you to settle the doubt, or win the argument with yourself. It offers a trade: the murky thing for the clear one, which is often sitting right beside it.
In al-Tirmidhi's version, a reason follows: truthfulness is tranquility, and falsehood is doubt. So the hadith points at something you can actually notice. What's true tends to sit still inside you.

What's off keeps nagging, like that smell. This is the rule of thumb for the gray zone in hadith six of the forty, where the heart was doing the steering. But there's a second half, and it matters just as much.
This isn't a rule for endless second-guessing. Another report, in Sahih al-Bukhari, is about someone in the middle of prayer who isn't sure whether their wudu has broken.
The answer: don't leave the prayer unless you hear a sound or notice a smell. A vague doubt doesn't cancel what you were sure of.
One to tell a friend tonight: the same tradition that says leave the doubt also says ignore the doubt, and the difference is whether there's real evidence or only a nagging thought.

how: Muslims use this hadith as a rule of thumb in gray areas, choosing the option that leaves no doubt; for doubts in worship such as wudu, teachers point to the report about a sound or a smell, so that certainty isn't undone by a vague worry.

games.q: what does “leave what makes you doubt” mean?
o: trade a doubtful thing for one that's clear
ignore your doubts and stick to the plan
doubt everything until you can prove it

games.q: the doubt, and the clear — tap the pairs.

s: 'leave what makes you doubt' means quitting whatever feels hard
it's about doubt over right and wrong: the murky thing traded for a clear one.
al-Tirmidhi's version adds: truthfulness is tranquility, falsehood is doubt
what's true tends to sit still in you; what's off keeps nagging.
the tradition says to act on every passing doubt
a report about wudu says don't leave the prayer unless you hear a sound or notice a smell.

games.q: halfway through prayer, a thought: has my wudu broken? you heard nothing and noticed nothing. what fits today's lesson?
o: keep praying: a vague doubt doesn't undo what you were sure of.
stop and redo wudu: leave what makes you doubt, always.
finish, then redo the whole prayer later, just in case.
games.why: the report in Sahih al-Bukhari: don't leave the prayer unless you hear a sound or notice a smell. leave the doubt means trade it for what's clear, not obey every nagging thought.

practice: Pour a glass of plain water, or hold one if it's near. Take one slow sip and notice how little there is to question in it: clear, cool, nothing hidden.
Keep the glass in your hand for the rest of the sit, and let one murky thing from your week sit beside it in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Leave what makes you doubt: trade the doubtful for what doesn't make you doubt. Truthfulness is tranquility; falsehood is doubt.

orig.s: دَعْ مَا يَرِيبُكَ إِلَى مَا لَا يَرِيبُكَ
orig.say: DA' maa ya-REE-buk i-laa maa laa ya-REE-buk
orig.note: Arabic: leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt.

carryVoice: Something to keep: leave the doubt, and take the clear thing sitting right beside it. That's thirteen days.

sources.ref: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 2518; Sunan al-Nasa'i 5711 (al-Hasan ibn Ali: leave what makes you doubt for what does not; truthfulness is tranquility, falsehood is doubt)
Sahih al-Bukhari 137; Sahih Muslim 361 (do not leave the prayer unless you hear a sound or notice a smell)
